blocks.content: {"text":"Daily Incision Checks"}

{"text":"✓ Check for redness or swelling
✓ Ensure incision is dry
✓ Monitor for discharge (clear serum normal first 48hrs)
✓ Ensure sutures/staples intact"}
{"text":"When to Call"}

{"text":"• Redness or swelling increasing
• Foul-smelling discharge
• Suture/staple dehiscence
• Discharge is thick, colored, or bloody
• Animal licking or chewing incision"}
{"text":"Activity Restrictions"}

{"text":"• Leash walks only for 10-14 days
• No running, jumping, or playing
• No swimming until sutures removed
• Crate rest when unsupervised"}
{"text":"Phase 1: Immediate Recovery (Days 1-3)"}

{"text":"1. Pain management continuation
2. Incision assessment
3. Limited mobility enforcement
4. Appetite monitoring"}
{"text":"Phase 2: Early Healing (Days 4-14)"}

{"text":"1. Gradual activity increase
2. Physical therapy exercises
3. Incision healing monitoring
4. Suture removal scheduling"}

3. Anti-inflammatory management
4. Recovery milestone tracking"}

{"text":"URGENT – Come straight down!"}
{"text":"About"}

{"text":"Foreign body obstruction is one of the more common and potentially life-threatening conditions in vet practice. An intestinal or stomach obstruction can compromise or cut off blood supply to vital tissues — if this happens, the tissue may die or be irreparable."}
{"text":"Common Items Ingested"}
{"text":"Tissues, articles of clothing (especially underwear & socks), sticks & rocks, food wrappers, bones, children's toys, condoms, hair ties (cats)."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}
{"text":"Patient will likely need bloodwork, X-rays, or surgery — admit as early in the day as possible."}
{"text":"Nurses will triage if a vet is not available. Inform the team the pet is coming down."}
{"text":"If eaten within the last 2 hours, we may induce vomiting (if safe)."}
{"text":"URGENT – Come straight down. An urgent consultation is required for any birthing difficulties."}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"Refer to the SharePoint document for detailed whelping advice to give clients over the phone."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! Death can occur in 1–2 hours. 🚑"}
{"text":"About"}
{"text":"Bloat occurs when a dog's stomach fills with gas, fluid, or food and expands. It becomes life-threatening when the stomach rotates (Gastric Dilation-Volvulus / GDV)."}
{"text":"Signs of GDV"}
{"text":"Non-productive retching / attempting to vomit."}
{"text":"Visibly bloated or distended abdomen."}
{"text":"Drooling, restlessness, panting, collapse."}
{"text":"At-Risk Breeds"}
{"text":"Great Danes, St. Bernards, Weimaraners, Irish Setters, Standard Poodles, Doberman Pinschers. Often occurs after eating. During desexing, a Gastropexy can be performed to prevent GDV."}
{"text":"Book with a senior vet if possible. Dog must be taken straight through to Hospital on arrival."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! If untreated within 24–48 hours, the cat can die. 🚑"}
{"text":"About"}

{"text":"Feline Lower Urinary Tract Disease (FLUTD) affects the urethra and bladder. A male cat that is not urinating freely requires immediate attention — a life-threatening urinary blockage may be present."}
{"text":"Key Points"}
{"text":"Owners often confuse a blocked bladder with constipation — the cat is seen straining in the tray but can't pee."}
{"text":"The cat may also be licking at their privates excessively."}
{"text":"The blockage causes acute kidney failure."}
{"text":"If a client says \"My cat is constipated\" — explain it's most likely they can't pee (if male) and they need to come down immediately."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"About"}
{"text":"Dogs cannot metabolise theobromine (the main toxin in chocolate). The darker the chocolate, the more toxic it is. Symptoms can take 6–12 hours to develop."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}
{"text":"Ask the client to bring the chocolate wrapper — it helps calculate theobromine ingested."}
{"text":"If eaten within 1–2 hours, the vet may induce vomiting."}
{"text":"Larger dogs can consume more before reaching toxic levels."}
{"text":"Chocolate Toxicity Calculator (guide only): https://petsci.co.uk/tools/chocolate-toxicity-calculator/ — All clients should still be advised to bring the patient in immediately."}
{"text":"RED – Come straight down!"}
{"text":"About"}

{"text":"Not all bite wounds tear the skin, but they can cause significant internal crushing damage. Even small punctures can mean significant internal trauma. All animals involved in dog attacks need to be seen immediately."}
{"text":"What to Expect"}
{"text":"Vet will perform a physical exam and may start life-saving interventions immediately."}
{"text":"Pain relief and antibiotics administered. Surgery is often required to debride and close wounds."}
{"text":"Puncture wounds can reach the abdomen (organ damage) or chest (lung puncture). Emergency surgery may be needed."}
{"text":"Blood tests and potentially a blood transfusion may be required for severe injuries."}
{"text":"Notify the Hospital Manager that this patient is coming down so they can be prepared."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! Not being able to breathe is not good! 🚑"}
{"text":"If Heatstroke — Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"If arrival will be delayed (waiting for transport, help lifting pet etc), ask the client to:"}
{"text":"Remove the pet from the hot environment immediately."}
{"text":"Apply tepid/cool (NOT ice-cold) water to fur and skin, then fan to maximise heat loss."}
{"text":"Wet down the area around the pet where possible."}
{"text":"Get to the clinic as soon as possible."}
{"text":"Potential Causes"}
{"text":"BOAS (Brachycephalic Airway Syndrome): French Bulldogs, Boxers, Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, Shih Tzus, Pekinese, Pugs — these breeds have shortened airways and overheat easily."}
{"text":"Heatstroke: Extremely dangerous and can be fatal."}
{"text":"Tell the Hospital Leader an animal is coming in with trouble breathing so they can prepare the hospital."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Toxic Foods"}
{"text":"Chocolate (see Chocolate Toxicity protocol), Onions, Garlic, Grapes, Sultanas, Macadamia Nuts."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}
{"text":"If eaten recently, the vet may induce vomiting."}
{"text":"IV fluids and other medications may be required depending on amount eaten and patient size/breed."}
{"text":"Animal Poisons Reference: https://animalpoisons.com.au/common-poisons"}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Signs of Heat Stroke"}
{"text":"Excessive panting, drooling, weakness, collapse, vomiting, diarrhea, seizures."}
{"text":"Immediate First Aid"}
{"text":"Remove from heat source immediately."}
{"text":"Apply cool (NOT ice-cold) water to body and fan."}
{"text":"Transport to clinic immediately."}
{"text":"Heat stroke is life-threatening and requires emergency treatment."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"Approach the animal with caution — an injured, frightened dog or cat may bite even if they know you."}
{"text":"Large dogs: carefully slide a board, blanket, or towel underneath to use as a stretcher. Always support the back."}
{"text":"Small dogs and cats: wrap in a towel to move. Don't wrap too tight."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}

{"text":"Even a small bump from a car can cause serious internal injuries that are not yet apparent. A ruptured diaphragm causes immediate lung collapse with no visible external injuries. All HBC patients should come straight down regardless of visible injuries. They may also need treatment for shock."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"About"}
{"text":"All parts of the Lily are toxic to cats — including pollen and leaves (flowers are most toxic). As little as two leaves or part of a flower can result in death."}
{"text":"Timeline"}
{"text":"Acute renal failure can occur within 12–18 hours of ingestion."}
{"text":"Sudden death has been reported after 6–8 hours (depending on amount consumed)."}
{"text":"If treated within 18 hours of exposure, the prognosis is good for the patient."}
{"text":"URGENT – Come down as soon as possible."}
{"text":"About"}
{"text":"Milk fever (eclampsia) is a metabolic emergency in nursing mothers, typically occurring 1-4 weeks after giving birth."}
{"text":"Signs"}
{"text":"Stiffness, tremors, muscle twitching, nervousness, panting, lethargy, loss of appetite."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}
{"text":"Requires immediate veterinary treatment with IV calcium."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Common Drugs Ingested"}

{"text":"Panadol (Paracetamol), Nurofen (Ibuprofen), Aspirin, Valium, Sleeping tablets, Blood pressure medication, Beta blockers, Benzodiazepines, Xanax, Antidepressants (Effexor, Prozac, Lexapro), ADHD medications (Ritalin), Birth control pills, Thyroid hormones, Statins, Marijuana."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}
{"text":"Ask the client to bring down the bottle/packaging."}
{"text":"If eaten recently, the vet may induce vomiting."}
{"text":"IV fluids and other medications may be required. Many of these can cause liver damage if not treated promptly."}
{"text":"Poisons Helpline: 1300 869 738 | Animal Poisons: https://animalpoisons.com.au/common-poisons"}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"About"}

{"text":"Rodenticides act as anticoagulants — they deplete the body's supply of vitamin K, which is essential for blood clotting. This causes internal bleeding, brain swelling, and high calcium levels (leading to kidney failure)."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}
{"text":"Death from internal bleeding: 3–7 days. Animals can remain symptom-free for many days, giving a false sense of reassurance."}
{"text":"Ask the client to bring down the rat bait packaging."}
{"text":"If eaten recently, the vet may induce vomiting."}
{"text":"Poisons Helpline: 1300 869 738"}
{"text":"URGENT but not an immediate emergency — come down when the seizure finishes and the dog is near normal again."}
{"text":"Advice if Animal is Currently Seizing"}
{"text":"Don't panic! Most seizures last only a minute or so. Remove anything nearby that could cause injury."}
{"text":"No need to hold or comfort them — let it run its course. If in a dangerous area (e.g. stairwell), gently move them to a safer spot."}
{"text":"No food or water — it can make it hard to breathe."}
{"text":"After the Seizure"}
{"text":"Keep the dog in a safe area and monitor through the post-ictal phase (lethargy, restlessness, wobbly, temporary blindness, possible aggression). Once mostly back to normal, bring them in."}
{"text":"Come down IMMEDIATELY if: seizure lasts > 5–10 minutes, seizures cluster together without recovery time, or more than 2 seizures in 24 hours."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! Waiting to monitor the situation reduces the chance of survival. 🚑"}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"Do NOT try to catch or kill the snake."}
{"text":"Keep the pet calm — over-excitement can worsen venom effects."}
{"text":"Carry the pet to the car to minimise movement."}
{"text":"If bite is on the face or neck, remove the collar as the area may swell."}
{"text":"At a safe distance, photograph the snake or note its pattern and colour to help identify it."}
{"text":"Signs of Snake Bite"}
{"text":"Sudden weakness/collapse, muscle shaking or twitching, difficulty blinking, vomiting, loss of bladder/bowel control, dilated pupils, paralysis, blood in urine."}
{"text":"Gold Coast Snake Catcher — Tony Harrison: 0401 263 296"}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"If you've removed the tick, please bring it in for identification in a sealed bag, jar, or container."}
{"text":"Do NOT offer any food or water."}
{"text":"About"}

{"text":"The paralysis tick is a pink, egg-shaped arachnid (~3–5mm). Early treatment is key — deterioration can occur within hours. Even after tick removal, pets can worsen for up to 3 days, and the poison remains active in the system for 1–2 weeks."}
{"text":"Early Signs"}
{"text":"Lethargy, reduced appetite, occasional vomiting."}
{"text":"Later Signs (URGENT)"}
{"text":"Wobbly gait (often back legs), reluctance to move or jump, change in bark or meow, cannot blink, difficulty breathing, change in heart rhythm, excessive drooling, complete paralysis."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"If the Dog is Seizing or Having Tremors"}
{"text":"Bring straight down to the clinic immediately."}
{"text":"If the Dog Has Just Licked the Toad"}

{"text":"Use a damp cloth to wipe the inside of the dog's mouth (especially the roof) to remove the toxin. Rinse the cloth under cool running water after every wipe. Continue for 10–20 minutes. Be cautious — dogs may bite. NEVER use a hose to flush the mouth — this can cause the dog to inhale water causing life-threatening pneumonia. Bring the dog to us immediately after wiping."}
{"text":"Symptoms"}
{"text":"Drooling and foaming, brick-red gum colour, vomiting, diarrhoea, loss of coordination, rapid or irregular heartbeat, seizures, collapse."}
{"text":"How Long Until Dangerous?"}
{"text":"The adult cane toad has enough toxin to kill an average-sized dog in as little as 15 minutes. The smaller the dog or cat, the more seriously affected they will be."}
{"text":"EMERGENCY – Come straight down! 🚑"}
{"text":"Advice to Clients — Controlling Bleeding"}
{"text":"1. Apply direct pressure using a clean cloth or towel."}
{"text":"2. Do not keep removing pressure to examine the wound."}
{"text":"3. Do not bathe the wound."}
{"text":"4. Bring someone with you so they can maintain pressure while you drive."}
{"text":"5. If bleeding is minimal, place the animal on a towel and come straight down. Drive calmly and safely."}
{"text":"Key Notes"}

{"text":"Small skin punctures are deceptive — the damage underneath can be far worse than on top. Dog jaws are extremely powerful and can crush muscles, penetrate the chest wall (lung collapse), or cause serious organ damage."}
{"text":"Ensure you tell the Hospital Leader that a wounded animal is coming down so they can be prepared."}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Pet has been bitten by an ant, bee, wasp etc."}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"RED OR ORANGE: Assess severity — determine if the pet is having an allergic reaction!"}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general appointment duration."}
{"text":"If the patient has swelling, vomiting/diarrhoea, or can't breathe, they must come down immediately — possible anaphylactic reaction!"}
{"text":"For Your Information"}

{"text":"Pet can be showing signs of pain and irritation eg licking or chewing at the area bitten, or limping/not weight bearing. The bite is usually in an area with little hair eg foot pads, belly or face/nose."}

{"text":"If the pet is showing signs of discomfort only or localised pain at the bite site (none of the serious symptoms above), we should still see the pet. The vet may choose to give an anti-histamine injection or pain relief to make the animal more comfortable."}
{"text":"Always recommend the patient be seen. Book an appointment as soon as possible — if there is no appointment, an urgent slot will need to be made and the client charged accordingly."}
{"text":"A patient may also present with lumps or hives on their body (all over, or in certain areas)."}
{"text":"If the Owner Can't or Won't Come In"}

{"text":"Owner can apply a cold compress (wrapped in a light tea towel) to the bite for up to 10 minutes and monitor the pet at home over the next 24 hours. They may also put the limb into a cold water foot bath if the foot was bitten."}
{"text":"It is important the client watches the pet for 24 hours. They must come down immediately or go to the Emergency Centre (if after hours) if any of these signs develop:"}
{"text":"Swelling on face."}
{"text":"Vomiting & diarrhoea."}
{"text":"Weakness."}
{"text":"Difficulty breathing."}
{"text":"Agitation."}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Pet is not interested in eating at all or will only eat small amounts. Their eating habits have changed. Pet may also be lethargic or showing no interest in activity."}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"Urgent — assess urgency by asking appropriate questions."}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general appointment duration."}
{"text":"Book an early appointment where possible in case further workup is required eg blood tests."}
{"text":"For Your Learning"}
{"text":"Loss of appetite in pets is a common symptom. The cause can be as simple as a mild stomach upset, but it could also be a sign of serious disease."}
{"text":"Common reasons for pets to be off their food:"}
{"text":"Dental issues."}
{"text":"Pain."}
{"text":"Nausea."}
{"text":"Stress."}
{"text":"Adverse reaction to drugs."}
{"text":"Internal obstructions."}
{"text":"Changes in the environment."}
{"text":"Kidney failure."}
{"text":"Pancreatitis."}
{"text":"Cancer."}
{"text":"Gastroenteritis."}
{"text":"Infection."}
{"text":"Questions to Ask"}
{"text":"How long has the pet been off food?"}
{"text":"Is the pet vomiting or having diarrhoea?"}
{"text":"Has the pet experienced weight loss?"}
{"text":"Does the pet have any underlying medical conditions?"}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Vomiting: Most commonly a reaction to a minor stomach upset but can be a sign of something serious."}
{"text":"Diarrhoea: Caused by a variety of factors, including dietary indiscretion, food allergies or sensitivities, infections, parasites, and certain medical conditions."}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"RED OR ORANGE: Assess severity."}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general appointment duration."}
{"text":"Vomiting should be seen as early as possible in case the patient needs working up."}
{"text":"When Is It Urgent?"}
{"text":"Blood in the vomit — must be seen straight away."}
{"text":"Bloody diarrhoea — must be seen straight away."}
{"text":"Heatstroke — if the animal is overheating and vomiting, this is a medical emergency."}
{"text":"Advice to Clients"}
{"text":"If diarrhoea is present — ask the client to bring in a sample if possible (clean plastic container or glass jar with lid). No need to refrigerate."}
{"text":"Some Causes (Not a Full List)"}
{"text":"Ate too much."}
{"text":"Ate too fast — regurgitation straight after eating."}
{"text":"Ate grass."}
{"text":"Diet change or food intolerance."}
{"text":"Viral infections."}
{"text":"Motion sickness."}
{"text":"Heatstroke."}
{"text":"Swallowed something toxic."}
{"text":"Sign of serious illness eg pancreatitis, liver issues, constipation, parvo, urine infection, kidney issues."}
{"text":"Possible Treatments"}
{"text":"Strongly depends on the cause of vomiting, but may include:"}
{"text":"Medication and sent home."}
{"text":"Admitted to hospital for further workup which may include blood tests, X-rays or ultrasound."}
{"text":"About Librela & Solensia"}
{"text":"Librela (dogs) and Solensia (cats) are monthly anti-NGF monoclonal antibody injections for osteoarthritis pain. Given once a month by injection at the clinic."}
{"text":"Booking Notes"}
{"text":"Book as a nurse appointment (no vet required for routine injections once established)."}
{"text":"First injection must be a vet consult to assess suitability and take baseline weight."}
{"text":"Note species clearly — Librela is dogs only, Solensia is cats only."}
{"text":"Check when their last injection was — ideally every 28–30 days."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Nurse consult (ongoing) / Vet consult (new patient)"}
{"text":"Duration: 15 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: Current weight, last injection date, any adverse reactions previously"}
{"text":"Description"}
{"text":"Behavioural concerns including aggression, anxiety, excessive barking, destructive behaviour, or other behavioural issues."}
{"text":"Urgency"}
{"text":"NON-URGENT — Routine consultation to assess and manage behavioural concerns."}
{"text":"Procedure"}
{"text":"Book with any vet — general or extended appointment duration depending on complexity."}
{"text":"A thorough assessment of the animal's history and environment is required."}
{"text":"Common Behavioural Issues"}
{"text":"Aggression towards people or other animals"}
{"text":"Anxiety or fear-based behaviours"}
{"text":"Excessive barking or vocalization"}
{"text":"Destructive behaviour"}
{"text":"Inappropriate toileting"}
{"text":"Compulsive behaviours"}
{"text":"Vaccine Types"}
{"text":"F3 (Core): Feline herpesvirus, calicivirus, panleukopenia — recommended for all cats."}
{"text":"FIV: Feline immunodeficiency virus — for outdoor or at-risk cats (requires initial course of 3)."}
{"text":"FeLV: Feline leukaemia virus — for at-risk cats."}
{"text":"Booking Notes"}
{"text":"Book as a vet consult — examination is required with vaccination."}
{"text":"Ask if the cat is indoor, outdoor, or has contact with other cats to determine which vaccines are needed."}
{"text":"Confirm last vaccination date — annual boosters for F3; FIV requires annual boosters after initial course."}
{"text":"If overdue > 1 year, vet will advise on restarting schedule."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Vet consult"}
{"text":"Duration: 20 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: Vaccination history, indoor/outdoor status, any health changes"}
{"text":"Triage Questions"}
{"text":"Is the pet having difficulty breathing or is the cough very severe? → Upgrade to same-day/urgent."}
{"text":"Is the pet lethargic, off food, or running a temperature? → Book same-day."}
{"text":"Mild cough, otherwise well → routine appointment is fine."}
{"text":"Kennel Cough (Bordetella / CIRD)"}
{"text":"Kennel cough is highly contagious. If suspected, advise the owner to keep the pet away from other dogs and call ahead when arriving so we can seat them away from other patients."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Vet consult"}
{"text":"Duration: 20 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: How long coughing, any contact with other dogs, vaccination status (esp. KC vaccine), eating/drinking normally"}
{"text":"If kennel cough suspected: note on appointment to seat away from other dogs on arrival."}
{"text":"Vaccine Types"}
{"text":"C3 (Core): Distemper, hepatitis (adenovirus), parvovirus."}
{"text":"C5: C3 + Bordetella + Parainfluenza (kennel cough) — required by most boarding/grooming facilities."}
{"text":"Leptospirosis: Available if at-risk."}
{"text":"Booking Notes"}
{"text":"Book as a vet consult — full examination required with vaccination."}
{"text":"Ask if the dog is boarded, goes to dog parks, or is in contact with other dogs — will determine if C5 is needed."}
{"text":"Confirm last vaccination date."}
{"text":"Puppies: 6–8 weeks (C3), 10–12 weeks (C5), 14–16 weeks (C3) — then annual."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Vet consult"}
{"text":"Duration: 20 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: Vaccination history, boarding/dog park exposure, any health changes"}
{"text":"Triage Questions"}
{"text":"Shaking head / scratching ear → routine appointment."}
{"text":"Tilting head to one side, falling over, or eye twitching → same-day (possible vestibular)."}
{"text":"Very painful ear, won't let you touch it → same-day."}
{"text":"Common Causes"}
{"text":"Ear infections (bacterial/yeast), ear mites (especially cats/puppies), grass seeds, polyps, or allergies are common presentations. A vet examination with otoscope is required to diagnose."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Vet consult"}
{"text":"Duration: 20 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: How long, which ear(s), any smell or discharge, previous ear issues, current medications"}
{"text":"Triage Questions"}
{"text":"Non-weight-bearing or sudden severe lameness → same-day appointment."}
{"text":"Mild limp, weight-bearing, no obvious wound → routine appointment."}
{"text":"Any swelling, wound, or visible deformity → same-day."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Vet consult"}
{"text":"Duration: 20–30 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required (advise light fast if sedation may be needed)"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: Which leg, how long, any known injury/trauma, getting worse or staying the same"}
{"text":"Triage Questions"}
{"text":"Facial swelling, hives all over body → urgent (possible allergic reaction)."}
{"text":"Scratching, licking, rash, hair loss, hotspot → routine appointment."}
{"text":"Common Causes"}
{"text":"Allergies (environmental, food, flea), bacterial/yeast pyoderma, mange, ringworm, hotspots. Vet will often take cytology samples for diagnosis."}
{"text":"Appointment Panel"}
{"text":"Appointment type: Vet consult"}
{"text":"Duration: 20 min"}
{"text":"Fasting: Not required"}
{"text":"Notes to collect: How long, location on body, any flea prevention used, diet, any previous skin history or allergies"}
{"text":"Triage Questions"}
{"text":"Cat straining and producing no urine → URGENT (possible blockage — life-threatening in male cats)."}
{"text":"Blood in urine, straining but still urinating → same-day."}
{"text":"Frequent urination, accidents, mild signs → routine appointment."}
{"text":"Urine Sample"}

{"text":"New research indicates that there are some benefits in delaying desexing for certain breeds. The research is inconclusive though, so until more information is available, we are still desexing at 5-9 months. You can however discuss the latest research with one of our vets to work out an age that is best suited for your pet, taking into consideration this new research."}

{"text":"If you wish to discuss it with a vet, I can go ahead and book you a Telehealth appointment which is cheaper than coming in ($55.00). If you didn't want to discuss it, our other choices are:"}

{"text":"Questions to Ask Before Making Appointment"}
{"text":"Female"}

{"text":"Is your dog currently in season? If yes — surgery should be delayed for 2 months. When an animal is in season, there is an increased blood supply to both the uterus and the ovaries. This can make the surgery more complicated."}
{"text":"Male"}

{"text":"Are both his testicles in the scrotum? If no — surgery is more complicated because the undescended testicle/s must be located first, and they are often much smaller in size. Exploratory surgery (opening the abdominal cavity) may be required, as the undescended testicle can be anywhere between the scrotum and the kidneys."}

{"text":"For Your Information"}

{"text":"There are various reasons why cats may need to be shaved, but the most common reasons are to remove matted hair, and to help keep cats cool during warmer weather. Cats with long coats should be brushed daily, but some cats don't tolerate brushing very well and make the process near impossible for their loving owners."}

{"text":"It's also difficult for long haired cats to regulate their body temperature on hot, humid days, so keeping their hair nice and short will help prevent them from overheating. Some cats have an extreme fear, or anxiety response to grooming procedures and will react with biting and scratching. This can lead to stress-induced health issues. To keep both your cat & our nurse safe, we only groom cats under anaesthetic."}

{"text":"While the groom itself is routine, there is no such thing as a routine anaesthetic or an easy anaesthetic. Putting an animal under anaesthetic is never without risk, so it's important for us to follow our usual procedures to ensure your cat will be as safe as possible while under anaesthetic."}

{"text":"A pre-anaesthetic blood test is compulsory for all cats over the age of 8 years. At the age of 8, cats are classed as Geriatric, and older animals can experience age-related changes in their organ function."}

{"text":"Impaired organ function can affect how the body processes and eliminates anaesthetic drugs, potentially increasing the risk of complications. By identifying potential health concerns before an anaesthetic is given, vets and pet owners can make informed decisions about whether to proceed."}

{"text":"If you are a new client and your cat has not been seen by one of our veterinarians, a consultation will be required prior to admission. We can book this in on the morning of your cat's groom. For existing clients, a consultation is not required if your cat has had a physical exam in the past 12 months and received a clean bill of health. For cats with underlying medical conditions, we must have seen your cat within the past 6 months."}

{"text":"Please make sure they have not had anything to eat after 10pm the night before the groom. It is safe for a cat to continue to drink overnight, but remove the water bowl in the morning when you wake up."}
